title: Epistemic Social Learning: Latent Behavioral Structure under Endogenous Multi-Agent Interaction
claim: Coupling fast per-interaction belief inference with slow shared-parameter updates creates a feedback loop between data generation and learned representations.
layout: 2 stacked bands (fast top, slow bottom), left-to-right steps, feedback arrows looping back
description: A dense system diagram on a white background. At left, a blue box for the Environment & Population shows an icon of a crowd of green figures, labeled N agents. A large green band on top is titled Fast Timescale: Epistemic Inference. It holds five boxes, F1 to F5: interaction, action selection, observe opponent, belief update, and store interaction. Each box has a small icon and equations, and green arrows link them left to right. Below it, a large purple band titled Slow Timescale: Prototype Adaptation holds three boxes, S1 to S3: batch buffer, belief-weighted aggregation, and prototype update. A thick green arrow marked Batch formation runs from the fast band down to the slow band. A purple arrow leads right to a blue Shared Prototypes box with colored dots. Green and gray feedback arrows return updated prototypes to the fast band and to the environment. A legend sits at bottom right. The eye goes first to the two colored bands.
caption: ESL: Two-timescale belief-driven prototype learning. At the fast timescale (top), agents maintain pairwise beliefs over shared prototypes and update them when opponent signals are observed. Only observed signals enter the prototype-learning buffer, together with the corresponding pre-update belief snapshots. At the slow timescale (bottom), batches of M observed records yield belief-weighted gradients for the shared prototype update. This induces a feedback loop: beliefs shape interaction behavior and data generation, while accumulated evidence updates the shared prototypes, which in turn influence future beliefs and interactions.
abstract: In multi-agent interaction, a learner's actions shape the observations from which it infers other agents' behavior. A behavioral model may predict these observations well yet support poor adaptation when opponents change. We introduce Epistemic Social Learning (ESL), which couples fast, interaction-specific Bayesian beliefs with slower online learning of population-shared behavioral prototypes. Belief-conditioned decisions influence subsequent observations and, in turn, the representations learned from them. Under explicit regularity and averaging assumptions, we provide a conditional stochastic-approximation characterization of these coupled dynamics. Across twelve synthetic $3\times3$ cooperative, coordination, and adversarial games, ESL achieves the lowest aggregate post-switch regret among the evaluated online latent-adaptation methods, including a switch-aware Bayesian filter. Additional experiments examine observation loss, noise, and asymmetric incentives. These findings illustrate how predictive fit can differ from decision-relevant adaptation under policy-dependent interaction.
